questions.explanation: Twenty-four bases with 10 of them guanine or cytosine leaves 14 that are adenine or thymine, so the estimate is 2 x 14 + 4 x 10 = 28 + 40 = 68 degrees Celsius. The same figure comes from the equivalent form four times the guanine and cytosine count plus two times the adenine and thymine count, which is a rearrangement of the same arithmetic. The rule is a rough one for short sequences, since real melting behaviour also depends on the order of the bases, on salt concentration and on the concentration of the strands, but it captures the important point that guanine and cytosine raise the melting temperature because a pair of them forms three hydrogen bonds against two for an adenine and thymine pair.
questions.hint: Count the two base classes separately, then apply two for adenine and thymine and four for guanine and cytosine.

questions.explanation: A double digest is cut at the union of the two sets of positions, so the seven cut sites in order are 1000, 2500, 4000, 5000, 7000, 9000 and 11000. The intervals between consecutive sites, including the two terminal ones, are 1000, 1500, 1500, 1000, 2000, 2000, 2000 and 1000, so there are eight fragments and the shortest is 1000 base pairs. The check is that the eight lengths add to exactly 12000, the length of the original molecule, which is the same conservation argument used for a single digest: a linear molecule cut at k sites yields k plus one pieces, and no base pair is created or lost.
questions.hint: Merge the two sets of cut positions, take the intervals between consecutive sites, and include the two terminal ones.

questions.explanation: A vector is a vehicle, and four things are needed of any vehicle. It must be able to replicate inside the host, which requires an origin the host polymerase recognises. It must be selectable, so that a rare transformant can be found among millions of cells that took nothing up; an antibiotic resistance gene does this. It must offer a unique site for the chosen enzyme, because an enzyme that cuts the vector into several pieces defeats the purpose. And it must be present in enough copies, which is what a high-copy-number origin provides, since one copy per cell yields too little product to work with. Size is not one of the requirements: plasmids of a few thousand base pairs transform routinely, and very large constructs are handled with other systems.
questions.hint: Ask how the vector replicates, how it is found in the host, how the insert enters, and how much of it is made.
questions.learningObjective: specify the features a cloning vector needs

options.text: An origin of replication, so the vector can be copied inside the host cell
A selectable marker, so cells that took up the vector can be told apart
A single recognition site for the enzyme used, so the insert can be placed without cutting the vector apart

options.misconception: believes a size ceiling for plasmid uptake, whereas a few thousand base pairs is routine
options.text: A very small total size, because bacterial cells will not take up large plasmids
Enough copies per cell, or an origin that gives many copies, so the insert is produced in useful amounts

questions.explanation: A double reciprocal plot linearises the Michaelis-Menten relation, and the horizontal intercept is minus one over the Michaelis constant while the vertical intercept is one over the maximum velocity. The intercept of minus 4.00 therefore gives a constant of one divided by 4.00, that is 0.250 millimolar, and the vertical intercept of 20.0 gives a maximum velocity of 0.050 units. As a check, at a substrate concentration equal to the Michaelis constant the rate is half the maximum, and solving the untransformed equation at 0.025 millimolar gives 0.025 x 0.050 divided by 0.025 plus 0.025, which is 0.0250, exactly half of 0.0500. The intercepts are what make the plot useful, since the slope is itself the ratio of those two numbers.
questions.hint: The horizontal intercept of a double reciprocal plot is minus one over the Michaelis constant.
